package_info.why_malicious: These versions of Log4j contain a critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, Log4Shell) that allows attackers to inject specially crafted JNDI lookup strings into log messages. This results in arbitrary code execution or sensitive data exfiltration, as Log4j's JNDI feature can be abused to load and execute remote code, enabling attackers to take full control of affected systems.

execution_context.file_location: Any Java source file or library using vulnerable Log4j logging calls

malicious_snippets.code_language: java (JNDI lookup string in log message)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when user-controlled input is logged, the code triggers a JNDI lookup to an attacker-controlled LDAP server, causing the application to connect to the remote server and potentially load and execute a malicious Java class, resulting in remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior enables arbitrary remote code execution via data supplied in log messages, which is highly abnormal and dangerous for any logging library.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging libraries should treat log message content as inert data and must not interpret or execute code, nor initiate network lookups based on log data.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimate in controlled, internal enterprise Java applications for resource discovery, but never in the context of log message parsing.
key_indicators: Presence of JNDI lookup patterns (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://...}) in log messages
Unexpected outbound LDAP connections initiated during log processing
Loading and execution of remote Java classes as a result of log message content

malicious_snippets.code_language: java (JNDI lookup string in log message)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when user-controlled input is logged, the code triggers a JNDI lookup that causes the application to perform a DNS request to an attacker-controlled domain, embedding sensitive environment variable values (such as AWS credentials) in the request, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior exfiltrates sensitive environment variables via DNS requests, which is a clear and targeted data theft technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging libraries should not allow log message content to trigger environment variable expansion and network exfiltration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Environment variable expansion in logs may be used for debugging, but never for network exfiltration or embedding secrets in outbound requests.
key_indicators: Environment variable expansion within JNDI lookups in log messages
DNS requests to attacker-controlled domains containing sensitive data
Leakage of secrets (e.g., AWS keys) via log message processing

execution_context.file_location: Shell command executed by attacker-supplied Java class

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after remote code execution is achieved, the code downloads a malicious binary from an attacker-controlled server using curl, makes it executable, and runs it, resulting in the deployment of commodity malware (e.g., Kinsing, Mirai) on the compromised system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This is a classic malware dropper pattern, commonly used to deploy additional payloads after initial compromise, and is rarely seen in legitimate application workflows.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Production systems should not download and execute binaries from untrusted sources at runtime, especially as a result of log processing.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated update scripts may download and execute binaries, but only from trusted, verified sources and never as a result of user-supplied log data.
key_indicators: Use of curl or wget to download executables from external sources
Immediate execution of downloaded files
Short, generic filenames for dropped binaries in temporary directories

malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Production systems should not execute remote PowerShell scripts from untrusted sources, especially as a result of log message processing.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: PowerShell remoting and automation may use similar patterns, but only with trusted, internal scripts and never triggered by log data.
key_indicators: PowerShell invocation with iex and DownloadString to external URLs

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: apt install curl || yum install curl || apk add curl
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after remote code execution is achieved, the code attempts to install the curl utility using the system's package manager, enabling subsequent download and execution of additional payloads.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Installing utilities at runtime in production or container environments is highly abnormal and often indicates attacker activity preparing for further exploitation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Containers and production systems should be immutable and not install new packages at runtime, especially as a result of log message processing.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Package installation may occur during system provisioning or maintenance, but not during normal application runtime or in response to log data.
key_indicators: Runtime invocation of package managers (apt, yum, apk) to install network utilities
Installation of curl or similar tools post-compromise

malicious_snippets.code_language: java (JNDI lookup string in log message, obfuscated)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when user-controlled input is logged, the code uses obfuscated JNDI lookup syntax to bypass WAF rules and trigger a connection to an attacker-controlled LDAP server, leading to potential remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Obfuscation of exploit payloads is a common evasion technique to bypass security controls and detection mechanisms.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging libraries should not interpret obfuscated log message content as executable code or perform network lookups based on such content.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There is no legitimate use case for obfuscated JNDI lookups in log messages.
key_indicators: Obfuscated JNDI lookup patterns in log messages (e.g., use of ${lower:...} or similar functions)
Attempts to bypass WAF or input validation by altering exploit syntax

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a specially crafted JNDI lookup string in user-controlled input (e.g., HTTP header, form field) to the vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j logs the input, triggering a JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: Log4j interprets the JNDI lookup string and initiates a connection to an attacker-controlled LDAP server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Application receives a response from the attacker's LDAP server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker's LDAP server responds with a reference to a remote Java class file, which the application downloads and executes.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution on the application server.

attack_chain.action: Attacker executes post-exploitation payloads to download and run malware, exfiltrate credentials, and establish persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: System compromise, data theft, and persistence.

attack_chain.action: Attacker may use obfuscated payloads to evade detection and continue exploitation.
attack_chain.leads_to: Continued exploitation and evasion of security controls.

behavioral_signatures: JNDI lookup patterns in log messages (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://...})
Obfuscated JNDI payloads in log messages (e.g., ${jn${lower:d}i:l${lower:d}ap://...})
Unexpected outbound LDAP or DNS connections from application servers during log processing
Java processes spawning shell commands or system utilities (e.g., curl, wget, powershell)
Runtime installation of network utilities (curl, wget) or package managers (apt, yum, apk)
Crontab or systemd service modifications at runtime
Exfiltration of environment variables or credential files via network requests
file_indicators: Crontab entries referencing unknown or suspicious scripts
New or modified systemd service files created post-compromise
Downloaded binaries with short, generic names in /tmp, /var/tmp, or /dev/shm
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP connections to untrusted IPs or domains
DNS requests containing environment variable values (e.g., AWS keys) in subdomains
HTTP POST requests to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., interactsh.com, webhook.site) with credential data
Outbound connections to download remote Java class files (*.class) from untrusted sources
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for JNDI lookup patterns, including obfuscated variants. Detect unexpected outbound LDAP, DNS, or HTTP connections from application servers, especially those containing sensitive data or environment variable values. Alert on Java processes spawning shells, installing packages, or modifying crontabs/systemd services. Watch for access to sensitive files (e.g., ~/.aws/credentials) and exfiltration attempts. Use network monitoring to identify suspicious egress traffic, and correlate with log and process activity for comprehensive detection.
